name: Olga Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a loader underground at the Kestrel gold mine, the kind we call a bogger, which scoops up the broken rock after a blast and carries it to the ore pass. Thirty-one years now, the last twelve as the lead operator on my shift. I go down the ramp at half six in a light vehicle, get my orders from the shift boss, and then it's hours of mucking out stopes, which are the open spaces where the ore's been blasted. I like being good at something hard, and I like the quiet down there between blasts. My shoulders are what's wearing out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Has the work changed much over the years?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Some. In the deep stopes they use remote loaders now, driven by someone sitting in a room on the surface with screens and a joystick. They asked me twice to train for it and I said no both times. My husband Marek drives the school bus, our son Tomas is a fitter here at Kestrel, and our daughter Lena has a hair salon in town. I've got a phone that makes calls, and that's all I need from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but quietly. Most of what they call AI hasn't reached the bottom of a gold mine anyway. I don't go online, so it would be just the crib room and the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I finish my four years and go. I was always planning to stop at sixty-two, my shoulders won't take much more than that. Nothing in this picture changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep my head down. Marek and I would keep paying off the last of the caravan loan and putting a little aside. Maybe I'd finally book the trip to see my sister in the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's just a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say it quietly. Why quietly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the young ones are all excited about this stuff, and there's no point raining on them. I've been around long enough to know you don't win arguments in the crib room. You just wait and see who was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at all you'd worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual. Gold price drops, company cuts a shift, that kind of thing. That's been the worry for thirty years and it has nothing to do with computers.

S0.say: Most of what they call AI hasn't reached the bottom of a gold mine anyway. I'd say I told you so, but quietly.
S0.think: It means I finish my four years and go at sixty-two, like I always planned. My shoulders won't take much more, and nothing here changes that.
S0.do: Keeps doing her shifts and keeps her head down. Keeps paying off the caravan loan with Marek, saves a little and books a trip to see her sister.
S0.feel: Calm; it's just a normal year.
S0.quote: I've been around long enough to know you don't win arguments in the crib room.
S0.fieldNote: Olga is set on retiring at sixty-two and measures every picture against that date. Her usual worries are the gold price and shift cuts, not technology. She avoids open arguments and prefers to wait and be proven right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, and the company will do what pays. That's how it's always been. I wouldn't blame anyone in particular, I'd just say we'll see how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between you and me, it means they'd stop asking me to train on the remote loaders and start telling me. I don't want to spend my last years sitting in a room with screens. And if I refuse a third time, I don't know if there's a seat for me underground anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts as long as there's a manual loader to drive, and I'd ask the shift boss straight out how long that might be. I'd start putting more aside, maybe an extra two hundred a month, in case I have to stop before sixty-two. I'm not doing any courses, I'll tell you that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the ground's moving under my feet a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't do a course. If it came to the course or leaving, which would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably leave. Tomas says I'm being stubborn and he's probably right. But I've been doing this for thirty-one years, I'm not going to learn joysticks at fifty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra two hundred a month come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek's fishing trips, my hairdresser, sorry Lena. We'd stop the takeaway on Fridays. It's small things, but they add up over a couple of years.

S1.say: It's business, and the company will do what pays, like it always has. I wouldn't blame anyone, I'd just say we'll see how it goes.
S1.think: They'd stop asking me to train on the remote loaders and start telling me. I don't want my last years in a room with screens, and if I refuse again, I don't know if there's a seat for me underground.
S1.do: Keeps driving a manual loader as long as one exists and asks the shift boss how long that will be. Saves an extra two hundred a month by cutting small treats and refuses to take courses.
S1.feel: Anxious, as if the ground is shifting under her.
S1.quote: I'm not going to learn joysticks at fifty-nine.
S1.fieldNote: For Olga, steady change is not mild, because the remote loaders already exist at her mine and she has refused them twice. Her public line is a shrug, but privately she knows the choice may soon be forced. She admits she would likely leave rather than retrain, and sees it as stubbornness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and that's not on any one person, it's just too fast for everyone. Somebody should slow it down, I suppose the government. I'd say that much and not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be sixty in 2028, two years before I planned to stop, with maybe three months saved. If robots do the loading and the maintenance, Tomas loses his job at the same time as me. That's both incomes from Kestrel gone in our family at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take whatever early retirement package they offered, the first one, before it gets worse. We'd stop everything that isn't food, power and the caravan loan. And I'd ask Lena if Marek and I could rent out the spare room or help in the salon, though I don't know how to cut hair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night with the calculator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to look for a job outside mining right away, maybe at the council or the power company. He's thirty-one and he's got a little one. It's him I'd lose sleep over more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd wait and see. Would you still?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with two years. Waiting is what you do when there's time. With this one, I'd grab the first package going, because the second one is always smaller.

S2.say: It's too fast, and that's not on any one person, it's too fast for everyone. Somebody should slow it down, I suppose the government.
S2.think: I'd be sixty, two years short of my plan, with maybe three months saved. If robots do the loading and the maintenance, Tomas loses his job too, so both our family's Kestrel incomes go at once.
S2.do: Takes the first early retirement package offered and cuts spending to food, power and the caravan loan. Asks her daughter about renting out the spare room or helping in the salon, and urges her son to find work outside mining.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep over the numbers.
S2.quote: Waiting is what you do when there's time.
S2.fieldNote: Olga's wait-and-see habit breaks under a two-year timeline, and she switches to grabbing the first package. Her biggest fear is for her son, who works at the same mine. Her blame stays vague and pragmatic even when the stakes are high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people to sort themselves out if they're sensible. The company should give fair packages and the government should help the young ones retrain. Nothing too dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2031 means I could probably make it to sixty-two in 2030 before it fully hits. It would be tight, and the last year or two might be ugly. But I could see myself getting out on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down, and I'd ask HR in writing for my retirement date to be locked in for 2030. I'd put every spare dollar into savings, trying to get from three months to six. And I'd push Tomas to get his electrical ticket while the company still pays for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the last one. I'd have a date to aim for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the ugly last year or two you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the last manual loader driver on site, with the robots doing the stopes next to me and everyone waiting for me to go. Like being the last one at a party who doesn't realise the lights are on. I'd hate that, but I'd do it for the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your mind about the remote loader training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, even now. Maybe if they paid me to sit in the room for one year and then retire, I'd do it. But I wouldn't like it.

S3.say: Five years is enough for sensible people to sort themselves out. The company should give fair packages and the government should help the young ones retrain.
S3.think: I could probably make it to sixty-two in 2030 before it fully hits, though the last year or two might be ugly. I could see myself getting out on my own terms.
S3.do: Keeps driving and asks HR in writing to lock in a 2030 retirement date. Saves every spare dollar to grow from three months to six, and pushes her son to get his electrical ticket while training is paid.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier with a date to aim for.
S3.quote: Like being the last one at a party who doesn't realise the lights are on.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is just enough for Olga's plan to survive, and she clings to her retirement date. She would put up with being sidelined for the money but won't change her mind about remote training. Her advice to her son is more flexible than her own choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty for people to adjust. I wouldn't make a fuss about it. The young ones will sort it out like we did when the old mine closed in the nineties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'm gone in 2030 like I planned, so it barely touches me. I'd worry about Tomas a little, but he's got time to change. It's the first picture since the dull one where I can just get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just keep doing my shifts until 2030 and retire as planned. We'd keep paying off the caravan and saving a little. I'd tell Tomas to think about where he wants to be in ten years, but I wouldn't push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little, and mostly for my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the old mine closing in the nineties. What happened then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred people lost their jobs in one week. Some moved away, some went to the gold mine, a few never worked again. I was one of the lucky ones, I got a loader seat here in 1995.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you feel any different if the robots arrived the day after you retired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd go and have a look at them at the open day, maybe. I'd probably think they drive too carefully, and then I'd go home and have a coffee.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty for people to adjust, so I wouldn't make a fuss. The young ones will sort it out like we did when the old mine closed in the nineties.
S4.think: I'm gone in 2030 like I planned, so it barely touches me. I'd worry about Tomas a little, but he's got time to change.
S4.do: Keeps doing her shifts until 2030 and retires as planned. Keeps paying off the caravan and saving a little, and gently encourages her son to think about his ten-year plan.
S4.feel: Only slightly uneasy, mostly for her son.
S4.quote: I'd probably think they drive too carefully, and then I'd go home and have a coffee.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Olga is out before it arrives and settles back into her familiar routine. Her memory of the nineties closure gives her a calm, been-there view of change. Her only lingering worry is Tomas, and even that she softens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because Tomas and I would both lose our jobs at Kestrel in the same year. What would help is a fair package for people over fifty-five that gets them to the pension, and real help for the young ones with families to find something else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we're good at that nobody counts. I can hear when a loader tyre's going soft before the gauge shows it. I don't know if a robot can do that, but I've saved the company a few thousand dollars in tyres doing it.

headlineQuote: I can hear when a loader tyre's going soft before the gauge shows it.
portrait: Olga Varga is a 58-year-old lead loader operator at an underground gold mine with thirty-one years in, who has twice refused training on remote loaders. She is pragmatic, blames no one in particular and prefers to wait and see. She is calm with the plateau but anxious with steady change, because the remote loaders are already at her mine. AGI in two years alarms her because it could take her job and her son's at once; with five or ten years she can hold on to her plan to retire at sixty-two.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her son would both lose their jobs at the same mine in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: A fair package that carries workers over fifty-five to their pension, and real help for younger workers with families to find new work.
